https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-sanct.text: The EU has added five individuals to its Russia sanctions list. The move was driven by Moscow’s “intensified strikes deliberately targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure” in Ukraine, according to a press release . The press release does not refer to a specific attack, but earlier this week Russia carried out one of its deadliest barrages on the Ukrainian capital, killing 17. In July, a similar attack in Kyiv killed 12. Among those included in the new sanctions is Ramil Badgutdinov — the head of a company that helps produce the Iskander-M ballistic missiles — and Aleksandr Dyukarev, head of the KrasMash plant that produces Sarmat ballistic missiles. Russia has not yet used Sarmat missiles in Ukraine, but Moscow has been testing them. Advertisement Advertisement The remaining individuals are directors of Russian defense companies involved in communications systems and “the development of software for unmanned aerial vehicles and space-related military technologies,” reads the press release . “With its army stalled on the battlefield, Moscow is further escalating its campaign of terror against civilians,” wrote EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas on X. “The EU must continue to intensify pressure on Russia until Moscow ends its war.”

The most serious incident was on Tuesday evening at a substation in Bergheim, west of Cologne. Launch devices were used to fire cables across overhead lines, causing a short circuit that forced five units of the nearby Niederaussem coal plant to temporarily disconnect from the network. Earlier the same day, a similar attack was carried out near the Jänschwalde plant in eastern Brandenburg. More than a dozen launch devices were found. On Thursday, a passer-by found similar unused devices at a substation in Dormagen, between Cologne and Düsseldorf. Police say the objects matched the launch gear used in the other incidents. This week, officers found explosives in the 48-year-old's home, while a special operations unit stormed a truck in a wood, some 100 kilometers (62 miles) away. The suspect was not found. Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate, Baden-Württemberg and North Rhine-Westphalia said the federal government must invest at least €2.5 billion ($2.9 billion) per year to boost maintenance. Germany's waterways, including the Rhine, play a key role in moving raw materials across the country, carrying more than 5% of all freight transported, They said politicians often focus on investing in roads and railways, while canals and rivers often get neglected. Over the summer, the Rhine became almost impassable at one key location and many ships plying the Rhine had to operate with much-reduced cargoes. Economists at the Kiel Institute for the World Economy estimated the drought would cause an economic loss of up to €2 billion. North Rhine-Westphalia's Transport Minister Viktor Haase called for new fleets of inland vessels that can reliably operate even in extreme low-water conditions. https://p.dw.com/p/5Ledd Skip next section Several rallies planned on eve of Saxony-Anhalt state election 09/05/2026 September 5, 2026 Several rallies planned on eve of Saxony-Anhalt state election Saxony-Anhalt holds its state election on Sunday Image: Peter Gercke/dpa/picture alliance Thousands of people are expected at rallies in eastern Germany's state of Saxony-Anhalt ahead of elections for a new regional parliament. Police said 12 events have been registered in the state capital, Magdeburg, with others in Halle. Most of the demonstrations are against the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, which is widely expected to receive the most support in Sunday's vote. Trade unions and civil society groups are organizing the largest rallies. Their events include a so-called democracy festival. The AfD will also hold its final campaign event in Magdeburg. The latest polls put the AfD at over 40% support, putting it on course to be the largest party in the state parliament by a wide margin. However, without an outright majority, the chance of the AfD forming a government will get messy as mainstream parties have ruled out a coalition with the far right. No smaller party expected to enter parliament has offered to formally support an AfD-led government. https://www.politico.eu/article/russias-.text: BRUSSELS — A Russian-designed nuclear power plant being built in Hungary that would be the country’s biggest source of electricity will miss its completion date by at least two years, internal documents obtained by POLITICO show. A confidential construction schedule from Rosatom, the Russian-owned company that's building the Paks II nuclear plant, puts the completion date at the end of December 2034, not 2032 as previously flagged. The delay is the latest in a series of hold-ups that have plagued the project since it was commissioned in 2014 by former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán and his ally, Russian President Vladimir Putin. Advertisement Advertisement Paks II is critical to the future of Hungary’s energy supply. It expands the Soviet-era Paks nuclear plant that already provides nearly half of the country’s electricity but which is currently due to be decommissioned between 2032 and 2037. The two new Rosatom reactors would more than replace that lost power, generating 2400 megawatts compared to the 2000 MW generated by the existing plant — enough to power a city of several million. But despite its key role in Hungary's future energy system, the plant's Russia connections made it controversial from the start, and Hungary’s new prime minister Péter Magyar — who replaced Orbán in April and is an open critic of Russia — has already placed it under review . The disclosure of the latest document — an Excel spreadsheet with thousands of cells — follows POLITICO's reporting on safety concerns at another Rosatom nuclear plant in Egypt that uses the same reactor technology as Paks II. In response to that story, Rosatom touted its “high standard of work” and “safety culture,” rejecting allegations of negligence during its ongoing build of the Egyptian nuclear facility. According to the spreadsheet document, the last of the two new reactors currently being built in Hungary will be ready for “provisional acceptance” by Dec. 30, 2034 — marking the moment when Rosatom would hand over the finished project to the Hungarian state-owned operator for final checks. That suggests the estimated €12.5 billion nuclear project is unlikely to be fully up and running until well into 2035, contradicting Budapest’s most recent public statement earlier this year — when Orbán was still in power — that Paks II would likely be finished between 2031 and 2032 . In an emailed statement, Rosatom said it would not comment on the spreadsheet document because it had not seen it. POLITICO did not share the document with the company to protect the identity of the people who obtained it. Advertisement Advertisement Rosatom said that under the current schedule agreed to with the “Hungarian side,” the reactors will be ready “within the timeframe” previously established, but did not provide a date. “To date, foundation work on Unit 5 is 80% complete and will be finished by the end of the year, at which point preparations will begin for the first concrete pour at Unit 6, where excavation of the pit is currently underway,” it said. The scheduling spreadsheet is part of a broader tranche of documents shared through an intelligence official who was granted anonymity because they are not authorized to speak to the media. Using other documents from the same official, POLITICO last month revealed safety issues and alleged “negligence” on the part of Rosatom as it builds a nuclear facility in Egypt using the same reactor technology destined for Paks II. Viktor Orbán speaks at a press conference in Budapest on July 22, 2026. | Attila Kisbenedek/AFP via Getty Images The Hungarian government declined to comment after several requests, while the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not reply directly, but earlier in the week issued a lengthy article accusing POLITICO of “fake” news and dismissing the allegations regarding Rosatom's construction issues. More delays Columns in the spreadsheet detail licensing and construction expectations dating back to 2015 — shortly after Paks II was announced in a 2014 deal between Orbán and Putin. One set of cells explains how the “first concrete on Unit 6” would occur on Sept. 6 this year, with the final regulatory milestones granting an “operation license” and the “provisional acceptance of Unit 6” by Dec. 30, 2034. Rosatom issued a press release after pouring its first concrete for the Unit 5 reactor in February, but according to the spreadsheet, that date was initially supposed to happen almost a year earlier in March 2025, meaning the project missed its targets by a year and could be further delayed beyond December 2034. Advertisement Advertisement Metadata analysis of the spreadsheet shows it was initially created in 2015 and updated over the last decade, but it is unclear when it was last amended. In late August, Putin held a meeting in the Kremlin celebrating the history of Russian nuclear industries and reassuring the world of Rosatom’s “solid track record of upholding high safety standards and ensuring the reliable operation of nuclear power plants” and applauding the “28 power units in its portfolio in various countries around the world.” In the same meeting with Putin, Rosatom CEO Alexei Likhachev delivered a keynote speech to other Russian officials and reiterated that “[projects] are progressing smoothly in India, China, Türkiye, Egypt, Iran, Bangladesh, and Hungary.” Rosatom is leading construction of Paks II, working alongside a network of contractors and suppliers from countries including Hungary, France and Russia. The project is overseen by Paks II Ltd., the Hungarian state-owned company responsible for the expansion. Rosatom and German engineering firm Siemens Energy ended their cooperation on the project after a protracted dispute over Berlin's failure to issue export approval for one of its companies to work with the Russian-led development. The termination was made public in February 2026. “Given the complexity of the investment, this is necessarily a time-consuming process, and we will be in a position to provide more detailed and precise information once the review has been completed,” a spokesperson for Paks II Ltd. said in a statement to POLITICO, referring to the Magyar government's review of the expansion project. In February, before Orbán's Fidesz party lost this year's national elections, Hungarian foreign minister Péter Szijjártó claimed in an interview that " 2031-32 " would "be completely realistic" for Paks II to come online. Szijjártó, who is under investigation for his ties to Russia during his time in office, announced his resignation from politics in July. Former Hungarian Green lawmaker Benedek Jávor , who focused on Paks II and was critical of the Orbán government, said he isn't surprised about the ongoing delays and thinks the Magyar government needs to act. “Hungary already spent around 1000 billion HUF (€2.7 billion) to this project,” he said. “The sooner the Hungarian government recognizes the unmanageable risks and abandons the project, the lower level of financial losses can be calculated.” Advertisement Advertisement

Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian The Guardian ‘Well-known individual’ tries to secure permanent injunction against Guardian and ITN Lawyers tell high court that client could harm himself if serious allegations against him are made public Michael Savage Media editor Fri 16 Oct 2026 14.20 EDT Last modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 14.22 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A “well-known individual” is trying to secure a permanent injunction against the Guardian and ITN to prevent them from publishing details of serious allegations made against him. At a high court hearing on Friday, the claimant’s legal team said there was a serious risk that he could harm himself should the allegations be made public. They have told the court publishing the claims would breach articles two and three of the European convention on human rights (ECHR), the former of which relates to the right to life. A trial is due to take place later this month to examine whether an injunction preventing reporting of the allegations should be made. An earlier ruling by the judge, Mr Justice Nicklin, said the case included two media organisations that had “conducted a journalistic investigation into allegations concerning the claimant’s conduct towards a number of individuals”. “The proposed publications concern serious allegations about the claimant’s conduct over a period of years,” it stated. “The matters alleged are said to have arisen in a variety of professional and personal contexts.” The judge explained that the claimant had given a broad denial of the allegations which the defendants propose to publish. In a submission to the court, the claimant’s legal team, led by Sara Mansoori KC, said he was “a well-known individual who suffers from very serious mental health problems”. The submission stated he had attempted to take his own life on two occasions and remained seriously ill. ITN and the Guardian are opposing the injunction sought. In their own written submission to the court, their legal team set out their position on the questions that fall to be decided at trial. In a skeleton argument, they said the relevant duties under the ECHR were not triggered and should not prevent publication, and in any event, mitigations could be put in place to protect the claimant. Nicklin said on Friday that it was important to have the proceedings as open as possible, adding: “This case is going to be controversial either way it is decided.” In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline on 988, chat on 988lifeline.org , or text HOME to 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14.
